title: Tuwo Shinkafa
author: Florence Madu
desc: Soft sticky rice cooked in stages, water added each time the last lot evaporates, then mashed when the grains melt under a spoon.
longDesc: Tuwo shinkafa is the rice swallow of the north and it works on a cycle rather than a ratio: cook the rice, let the water evaporate, test a grain, add more water, repeat. The variety is the thing that matters — it has to be a soft rice that becomes sticky when cooked, because a firm long grain will never mash. When the grains show no resistance at all and melt when you press them, they are mashed with a wooden spatula, steamed covered for two minutes and wrapped. No quantities appear anywhere on the source page, which is flagged rather than filled.
ingredients: Short or medium grain soft rice — a variety that becomes sticky when cooked
Water, enough to cook the rice till very soft and sticky, added in stages
steps: Wash the rice and put it in a pot with water, on medium heat.
When the first water evaporates, test a grain for softness.
Add more water and repeat the cycle until the grains show no resistance at all.
The rice is ready when the grains melt when you press on them.
Mash with a wooden spatula until smooth and sticky.
Wrap portions in plastic film to stop them drying out.
chefTips: The variety is everything. It has to be a soft rice that goes sticky — a firm long grain or basmati will never mash into a swallow.
Melting under the press is the cue, and it is a texture test rather than a time. The source gives no timing at all and that is honest for rice that varies this much.
Add water in stages, not all at once. Each cycle takes the grains a little softer and lets you judge where you are.
No tiny resistance is the phrase to aim for. If you can feel the grain's structure at all, keep going.
The two-minute covered steam after mashing is what makes it smooth rather than grainy.
Wrap it while hot. Tuwo skins over fast and the film is what keeps it pliable.

No quantities are published anywhere for this dish. Two cups of soft rice to roughly five or six cups of water added in stages is a reasonable starting point, but that is a suggestion rather than a sourced ratio.
commonMistakes: Adding all the water at the start.
Mashing while the grains still have structure.
Leaving it unwrapped to dry out.
sources: Adapted from 'How to Make Tuwo Shinkafa', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Headnote as printed: 'Tuwo Shinkafa is a northern Nigerian fufu recipe that is prepared with the soft rice variety. It is usually served with Northern Nigerian soups: Miyan Kuka, Miyan Taushe etc.'

NO QUANTITIES ARE GIVEN ON THIS PAGE. The ingredient list is exactly two qualitative lines: 'Short/Medium grain soft rice' and 'Water (enough quantity to cook the rice till very soft and sticky)'. This is a flat gap in the most-cited source for the dish, and it is recorded as a finding. The starting point suggested in the tips is labelled as a suggestion, not as sourced.
The distinguishing specification, as printed, typo included: 'The rice used for Tuwo Shinkafa should be the a soft rice variety that becomes sticky when cooked.'

The method is as printed: cook the rice with water on medium heat; when the first water evaporates, test grain softness; add water incrementally and repeat the cycle; mash with a wooden spatula once the grains 'melt when you press on it'; steam covered 2 minutes; wrap portions in plastic film to stop them drying.

DONENESS CUE, as printed: the grains show 'no tiny resistance' when pressed and eventually 'melt'. A texture cue, not a time — and for rice whose cooking depends entirely on variety and age, that is the right kind of instruction.
THE PAGE MAKES NO COMPARISON to tuwo masara or tuwo dawa. No source consulted sets the three tuwos side by side.

On the evidence available, what distinguishes the tuwos is the grain and the technique that follows: this one starts from whole grains cooked and mashed; tuwo masara starts from a dry flour stirred into water (NGA085). TUWO DAWA, the guinea corn version, returned NOTHING from any named source and is not published in this collection — the record is empty.

A LEAD NOT RETRIEVED: Daily Trust's 'Sinasir (Rice Pancakes)' may carry the fermentation time that the sinasir record lacks, which is the reason sinasir is also not published here. See the note at NGA095.
reheating: Steam 5 minutes, or microwave in the film.
healthBenefits: Rice is easy to digest, which is part of why tuwo is given to the unwell.
culturalNote: Tuwo shinkafa is the standard accompaniment to the northern miyan soups and the thing a northern household eats most evenings. The absence of a written ratio is not carelessness — the rice variety, its age and its dryness all change what it needs, and the cycle of cook, test, add water is how anyone who makes it actually works.
